description:
We are NasaTwisters, a team from Monterrey, Mexico, who built FlameTrace for the "Flame in Freefall" challenge. We share an interest in space exploration, trustworthy AI and data you can verify.

We believe AI should make science more reliable, not less: every number we show comes from code and traces back to NASA's data, we would welcome people with experience in combustion or fire-safety engineering, machine-learning evaluation, and UX design to keep improving FlameTrace.
summary:
FlameTrace is an AI-assisted web dashboard (flametrace.world) that summarizes, ranks and interprets NASA's microgravity combustion investigations from the PSI repository (24 investigations, 1,982 tests) to deliver fire-safety insights for spacecraft, space stations, lunar and Martian bases, and rovers.

Three AI agents work on NASA's data: an Investigator summarizes and classifies each investigation, a Calculator answers fire-safety questions by running code on the test tables, and an independent Auditor recalculates every value and assigns a confidence grade. The AI decides what to compute; code computes it, so no number comes from a model's memory. Every finding shows its proof chain: claim, calculation, table rows and DOI.

This matters because in crewed missions a confident but wrong number can cost lives. FlameTrace makes every insight traceable and shows knowledge gaps honestly: when NASA has no data, for example on partial gravity, it says so instead of guessing.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

FlameTrace is a web dashboard that summarizes, ranks and interprets NASA's microgravity combustion investigations from the Physical Science Informatics (PSI) repository (24 investigations, 1,982 tests) to deliver fire-safety insights for crewed missions: spacecraft, space stations, lunar and Martian bases, and pressurized rovers.

Our core principle is that every result can be checked. Large language models can state numbers with confidence that are simply wrong, and in fire safety for crewed missions that is unacceptable. So in FlameTrace, the AI decides what to compute, and code computes it. No number on the dashboard comes from a model's memory.

HOW IT WORKS

A pipeline of three AI agents works on NASA's public data:

1. Investigator: reads each PSI investigation and writes a structured record (student and professional summaries, the main fire-safety pillar it supports: prevention, detection or suppression, and the crewed environments it applies to). Every statement must cite the PSI field it comes from; a validator in code rejects anything without a source.

2. Calculator: answers a fire-safety question by choosing a tested calculation from a catalog, or writing one read-only SQL query. Python runs it on the test tables and records the exact rows used. The model writes the explanation, and a checker rejects any number in the text that the calculation did not produce.

3. Auditor: independently recalculates every value with separate code and runs ten checks: format, traceability to real rows and DOIs, fidelity to the original cells, recalculation, units and physical ranges, number of supporting tests, whether the claim stays inside the conditions actually tested, data quality, faithful text, and charts. For the text review it uses an open model from a different family (Google's Gemma 4, running locally), on purpose, so the two agents do not share the same mistakes. That model only answers a fixed yes/no checklist with structured output; code answers everything numeric.

The result is a confidence grade (A, B, C, No data, or Rejected) that no model chooses: it comes from checks anyone can repeat. Model alerts can only be dismissed by a person, with their name and reason, and code checks can never be dismissed.

THE DASHBOARD

- Findings, each with its confidence grade, its checks and its proof chain: claim, calculation, table rows, DOI.

- Two views: student (plain language) and professional (fuel, configuration, conditions, measurements).

- Investigations browser, and coverage gaps that show what NASA has not tested yet.

- An interpretation lab that shows whether a result holds under a different reasonable reading of the data, clearly labeled as exploration, not a finding.

- 3D station and habitat models, and an opening that starts from our home, Monterrey, Mexico.

- A research assistant (chat) that answers questions by querying the data with tools; before an answer is shown, code verifies that every number exists in the tool results. It runs on an open model on our own GPU and is offline on the public site by design, for security: no exposed machine, no API keys in the browser, and no questions sent to third-party AI services.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- Researchers, engineers, professors and students can find the most relevant investigations for each crewed environment in minutes instead of reading dozens of datasets.

- Every insight is traceable to NASA's original data, so it can be trusted, cited and reproduced.

- "No data" is never shown as zero: if no test covers a condition (for example 30% oxygen for solid materials, the lunar habitat atmosphere), the dashboard shows it as a knowledge gap instead of calling it safe. PSI has no partial-gravity data, and the system says so instead of extrapolating to the Moon or Mars.

- Those gaps point directly to the experiments still needed for lunar and Martian fire safety.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Trust: numbers only from code, every claim cited, no silent extrapolation.

- Audiences: separate language for students and for professionals.

- Security and privacy: the AI chat runs locally and is not exposed to the internet.

- Cost: open models, free tiers and local hardware.

- Prompt-injection safety: text inside NASA records is treated as data, never as instructions, and each agent can only run the commands its job needs.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

Languages: Python, JavaScript, SQL.

Data and backend: NASA PSI, DuckDB, Supabase (Postgres), FastAPI.

AI: Claude Code (Investigator and Calculator agents), Gemma 4 with Ollama (Auditor text checks and the research assistant).

Frontend: React, Vite, three.js, Vega-Lite, deployed on Vercel at flametrace.world.

Hardware: the team's laptops and an NVIDIA RTX 4060 GPU for the local model.
